.agents/instructions/bootstrap.md.content:
# Complete project setup before implementation

This gate applies until `.agents/PROJECT.md` and `.agents/ARCHITECTURE.md` are
complete. It does not block answering questions, reading code, or preparing the
setup documents. Missing setup does block product-code changes, installing
dependencies, migrations, app/server launches, and unrelated configuration edits.

1. Read existing README, agent guidance, manifests, relevant source entry points,
   and test configuration without executing project code. Reuse existing docs
   through links instead of creating competing architecture descriptions.
2. Replace required placeholders with verified facts and source paths. Clearly
   distinguish observed behavior, explicit user requirements, and proposed design.
   Do not guess business purpose, desired scope, secrets, or architectural consent.
3. Ask one concise batch of questions for missing purpose, scope, stack, constraints,
   or design decisions. Existing authorization and explicit preferences remain
   valid; do not ask for information already established by the user or source.
   For a new project, agree on the proposed architecture before marking it ready.
4. If questions cannot be asked or answered, report each unresolved field with its
   file path and the input needed. Leave status pending and do not implement the
   requested feature. In read-only tasks, propose documentation text in the reply
   instead of writing files without authorization.
5. Mark each document `Status: ready` only after all its required fields are
   resolved, evidence is cited, and no required placeholders remain. Record
   unavailable or inapplicable checks explicitly with a reason, rather than
   inventing commands or results. Then resume the authorized task.

`contextrivet project status` checks the scaffold's required sections, markers,
and files. It cannot verify the truth of documentation or enforce agent behavior.
If docs later become inaccurate, correct them from evidence; ask only about
decisions that materially affect the current task.

.agents/instructions/code-intelligence.m.content:
# Code Intelligence

For explicit architecture investigations, cross-module tracing, call/dependency
analysis, or security reviews that require understanding how code paths connect,
start with one or two targeted Codebase Memory MCP (CBM) graph queries when the
selected project has a current index and CBM is available. Use the results to
identify relevant symbols and files, then verify conclusions in source. Do not
request a whole-graph dump.

For a simple, local change or question whose answer is clear from a small number
of files, use direct source navigation without invoking CBM. If CBM is unavailable,
the project is not indexed, or graph results are inconclusive, fall back to targeted
source search and reads; do not silently create or refresh an index.

Keep retrieval proportional to the task. Avoid repeating equivalent queries,
pulling large neighborhoods without a concrete question, or reading broad
reports when a focused symbol/dependency result is enough. Follow returned file
paths to the source and read only the relevant ranges.

Treat graph results as navigation hints, not authoritative source. Verify
framework-mediated relationships, security-sensitive behavior, and ambiguous or
high-impact conclusions in the actual implementation, configuration, and tests.

Before relying on a result, confirm that CBM has an index for the selected
project and that its reported status is current enough for the task. If the
project is missing or the index appears stale, do not silently index or refresh
it; ask before changing index state when needed. Fall back to direct source
navigation and targeted search when CBM is unavailable or inconclusive.

Graphify remains an optional alternative only when explicitly requested. Do not
run both indexing systems automatically or treat either graph as a replacement
for project documentation or source code.

Project-specific `AGENTS.md` instructions retain their normal precedence. A
project may add an intelligence note when its owner chooses to; never create or
modify project files for this guidance automatically.

.agents/instructions/engineering.md.content:
# Shared engineering principles

- Prefer the smallest complete, maintainable solution. Inspect relevant code,
  callers, tests, contracts, and error paths before changing them.
- Apply SOLID where it clarifies responsibilities and real dependency boundaries:
  give modules cohesive responsibilities, keep contracts substitutable, expose
  focused interfaces, and keep business rules independent of concrete I/O.
  Do not add interfaces, layers, or factories without a demonstrated need.
- For new projects, prefer feature-first organization: keep a feature's behavior,
  state, UI or endpoints, data access, and tests close together where the framework
  permits. Document shared infrastructure and allowed cross-feature dependencies.
- Preserve a working project's established architecture. Document it first;
  propose restructuring only when requested or necessary for the authorized task.
  Feature-first organization does not require identical folders across stacks.
- Reuse installed dependencies and existing components. Keep shared code focused
  on actual reuse; avoid catch-all utilities and speculative framework building.
- Preserve validation, authentication, authorization, accessibility, data integrity,
  error handling, and compatibility. Keep credentials out of source and notes.
- Do not launch apps, servers, emulators, or physical-device debug sessions unless
  explicitly requested. Use permitted focused checks and explain manual testing.
- Follow Conventional Commits when asked to commit. Base proposed messages on
  staged changes; never stage or commit unrelated user work.

.agents/instructions/stack.md.content:
# Flutter guidance

- For new codebases, group screens/widgets, feature state, business behavior, and
  data integration by feature. Separate domain rules from Flutter/plugin I/O when
  that boundary has a concrete purpose; avoid empty mandatory layers.
- Reuse the project's state management, navigation, dependency injection, and
  design system. Do not select replacement packages during scaffolding.
- Document app startup, navigation, state ownership, persistence/network flow,
  and platform integrations. Preserve lifecycle handling and accessibility.
- Record focused analysis/test commands and physical-device checks. Do not run
  the app, emulator, or device debug sessions unless the user asks.

.agents/instructions/workflow.md.content:
# Task workflow and durable knowledge

## Before and during a task

- Check the onboarding gate in the canonical instructions. Read project context
  and architecture, then search the knowledge index for the affected feature.
- Verify notes against current source and tests. Source describes observed
  implementation; explicit user requirements describe intended behavior. Resolve
  material conflicts instead of silently treating either as universally correct.
- Trace only the paths needed for the task. Use the existing architecture and
  framework conventions; implement the complete authorized change and its edge
  cases without speculative cleanup.

## Save useful findings

- During authorized implementation or documentation work, update affected feature
  notes when you discover durable, non-obvious facts, pitfalls, or changed behavior.
  During read-only analysis/review, suggest the note update in the reply unless
  documentation writes are also authorized. Do not edit memory merely to answer
  a question, or write a note for every tool call.
- Create `.agents/knowledge/features/<feature>.md` only for an actual feature.
  Use `.agents/templates/feature.md` as a starting point and add its path plus a
  one-line purpose to `.agents/knowledge/INDEX.md`.
- Cite source paths/symbols, the review date, evidence, and relevant tests. Mark
  observations, accepted decisions, open questions, and unverified assumptions
  separately. Do not record guesses as project rules.
- Update existing entries rather than accumulating contradictory duplicates.
  Remove or supersede stale claims and fix index links after renames/removals.
  Keep current behavior concise; put durable rationale in
  `.agents/knowledge/decisions.md` and link from architecture when relevant.
- Never store credentials, tokens, private user data, environment dumps, or entire
  transcripts. Knowledge files are repository content and may be committed.

## Finish

- Run only checks allowed by project instructions. State what changed, what was
  checked, what remains uncertain, and practical manual/device verification steps.
- Update architecture/context only if the task changes their documented facts.
  Do not claim that tests passed, an agent loaded a skill, or an index refreshed
  unless there is observable evidence.

Team customization: keep schedule notes and offline data private.

Read only notes relevant to the current task. Verify claims against their cited
source before reuse. This index is navigation, not an automatic memory service.

- `.agents/knowledge/decisions.md` — accepted decisions and their rationale.

Add feature entries here as they are documented. Create feature notes under
`.agents/knowledge/features/` only when needed; start from
`.agents/templates/feature.md`. Avoid duplicating project context or architecture.

- `.agents/knowledge/features/schedule.md` — offline schedule observations

.agents/knowledge/decisions.md.content:
# Accepted decisions

No project decisions have been recorded yet. Add a decision only after it is
established by inspected code or explicit user agreement. For each, record:

- Date and status: observed, accepted, or superseded.
- Context and the decision, including who/what established it.
- Rationale and meaningful tradeoffs.
- Source paths, affected features, and a replacement link if superseded.

Keep proposals and unresolved questions separate from accepted decisions.

Stack profile: flutter

GitHub references below are not downloaded or installed by init.
Install selected skills with `contextrivet project skills install --names <name,...>`.
Use locally installed skills when relevant; a catalog entry does not prove activation.

- flutter-api-auth: Implement or fix Flutter REST/API integration, authentication sessions, token refresh, request retries, cancellation, pagination, and cache isolation. Use for network/session behavior; preserve the project's HTTP client and auth provider. — <https://github.com/Shahzad-Official/flutter-skills/tree/7930b9420c45adf1b162255a33f2c4fc1d55356c/flutter-api-auth>
- flutter-architecture: Design or scaffold Flutter projects and features, layer boundaries, state management, and dependency injection. Use for architecture decisions; preserve existing project conventions unless a migration is requested. — <https://github.com/Shahzad-Official/flutter-skills/tree/7930b9420c45adf1b162255a33f2c4fc1d55356c/flutter-architecture>
- flutter-async-state-safety: Diagnose and fix Flutter/Dart race conditions, stale UI or caches, overlapping requests, optimistic updates, and lifecycle bugs in Bloc, Cubit, Riverpod, or widget state. Use when async ordering or state ownership is implicated, including during an audit-and-fix task. — <https://github.com/Shahzad-Official/flutter-skills/tree/7930b9420c45adf1b162255a33f2c4fc1d55356c/flutter-async-state-safety>
- flutter-codebase-audit: Review Flutter or Dart code for concrete security, correctness, async/state, performance, and maintainability issues. Use for audits and production-readiness reviews; implement fixes when the user also asks to fix them. — <https://github.com/Shahzad-Official/flutter-skills/tree/7930b9420c45adf1b162255a33f2c4fc1d55356c/flutter-codebase-audit>
- flutter-firebase-workflows: Implement or fix Flutter Firebase Auth, Firestore, Storage, and callable-function behavior, including rules boundaries, listener lifetimes, offline data, and concurrent writes. Apply only when the project actually uses Firebase. — <https://github.com/Shahzad-Official/flutter-skills/tree/7930b9420c45adf1b162255a33f2c4fc1d55356c/flutter-firebase-workflows>
- flutter-release-readiness: Review or prepare Flutter Android/iOS release configuration, flavors, permissions, signing references, and device verification. Use for release/build readiness work, not as a mandatory checklist for every feature edit. — <https://github.com/Shahzad-Official/flutter-skills/tree/7930b9420c45adf1b162255a33f2c4fc1d55356c/flutter-release-readiness>
- flutter-tdd-workflow: Implement Flutter or Dart behavior with red-green-refactor when the user explicitly requests TDD or the project requires test-first development. Includes deterministic async race and stale-state regressions without imposing TDD on unrelated tasks. — <https://github.com/Shahzad-Official/flutter-skills/tree/7930b9420c45adf1b162255a33f2c4fc1d55356c/flutter-tdd-workflow>
- flutter-ui-quality: Build or fix Flutter screen behavior, responsive layouts, forms, keyboard/focus handling, accessibility, localization, and loading/error/empty states. Use for UI work and concrete UI defects, reusing the app's design system. — <https://github.com/Shahzad-Official/flutter-skills/tree/7930b9420c45adf1b162255a33f2c4fc1d55356c/flutter-ui-quality>

.agents/skills/ponytail/SKILL.md.content:
---
name: ponytail
description: >
  Prefer the smallest complete code change for implementation, refactoring,
  debugging, and reviews of actual or proposed changes. Use when the task benefits
  from avoiding unnecessary dependencies or abstractions. Do not load solely for
  read-only architecture investigations. Modes: lite, full, ultra.
argument-hint: "[lite|full|ultra]"
license: MIT
---

# Ponytail

Adapted from https://github.com/dietrichgebert/ponytail (MIT licensed).

Solve the complete task with the least new code that is easy to maintain.
Inspect the relevant code before changing it and identify affected callers,
tests, configuration, exports, and any data or security consequences.

1. Skip unrequested speculative features.
2. Reuse existing project patterns and components first.
3. Prefer built-in platform features or already installed dependencies.
4. Introduce an abstraction only when it solves a demonstrated need.
5. Finish the entire necessary change, including affected tests and fixtures.
6. Preserve intentional architectural boundaries, validation, security, and accessibility.
7. For nontrivial logic, include a focused test or equivalent check where appropriate.
8. In the final reply, state any skipped verification and material risks concisely.

Modes: lite (give the minimal viable approach and a smaller alternative),
full (apply all rules), ultra (also question unnecessary requirements).

Team customization: keep schedule notes and offline data private.
